utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are present. The Prosecution team is composed of Mr. McCloskey only today. Amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic; Mr. Lazarevic, I don't see him there; Mr. Krgovic; and that's it. Good morning to you, Colonel Landry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal where you are going to give testimony as an expert witness summoned by the Defence team for Accused Nikolic. Before you do so, our Rules require that you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth. The text is going to be handed to you. I don't know whether it's in English or in French. In either language, please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Messr. Landry. Make yourself comfortable. It was decided a couple of days ago that because of the subject matter of your testimony, same will be received in private session. Reason is that if we don't, we will have to move from private to public like a yo-yo throughout the whole testimony, and that will not be convenient or acceptable to anyone because the public sessions themselves would not make any sense. It was put to the parties to come to an agreement on this, and they have both agreed that it is best if we hear your evidence in private session. First, you are going to be asked questions by Mr. Bourgon, I notice, and you will then -- he will then be followed by others on cross-examination. So shall we stay in open session for the first part, and then you tell us, Mr. Bourgon, when to move into private session. I am using private session because, otherwise, with closed session, we'd have to bring down the curtains and I think we can still live with a private session without having to feel further suffocated in here. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. Good morning, colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this testimony will be done entirely in French. I'll be asking the questions and the witness will be answering in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. For me and Judge Prost, I will probably be following the testimony in French anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Colonel, my first question is very simple: Should we call you Mr., sir, Professor, or Colonel?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: You can call me "sir," but you can call me whatever you feel more comfortable in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you please give us your name?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Remi Landry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Fifty-seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: 1st of April 1951.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Colonel, before we begin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Un moment, s'il vous plait. If you could explain also to the witness why I have asked you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Colonel, before we begin, I would like to remind you that since we both speak the same language, it is very important that you wait before you answer. You wait for me to put the question to you before you answer immediately. So do you understand?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would also like to remind you that it is very important not to speak too fast in order to enable interpreters to faithfully interpret what you are saying into English and into B/C/S. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I see that you brought with you a large amount of documents. What are these documents?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Well, I brought my report that I sent to you. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, redact straightaway. I think, Mr. Bourgon, please use your discretion. The witness should know that he shouldn't be mentioning any names in open session, at least he has to refrain of doing that a until we are in private session; otherwise, we go into private session straightaway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, as the Presiding Judge just explained it to you, until we are in closed session, I would like to ask you not to mention any names, please.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I shall do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You said that you brought your report with you. Do you have a copy of your report in English and in French?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have a French copy and an English copy of my report, and they are both with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you have other documents other than the documents that you mentioned to me, so a copy of the these two reports of your report, as well as the document that we have given you?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I have some notes helping me to answer to your questions and some notes I took, so that will help me through my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I already explained to you that all the notes that you have brought with you were already given to the Prosecutor. Can you please tell us in what language your report was drafted originally?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: In French.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you able so far to check the English translation of your report?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. I had the occasion to peruse through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what is the impression you had?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Upon checking the report, I see that it seems to reflect very well my French report, but I must note that the English report is followed by my electronic signature, and I just wanted to make absolutely certain that I'm not the author of this translation. I did not translate this report. And I also noted some small discrepancies, and also some terms were not interpreted or translated exactly as they should. So there are some discrepancy between the French and English report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. I would like to hand you a document bearing number 3D504, and I would like you to tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's a list that was uploaded in e-court yesterday, but it was not yet available on e-court. I will ask the court usher to give a paper copy, so everybody in the courtroom has received a copy of this proposed exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you to put that exhibit on the ELMO, this way everybody will be able to see it. What is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: This is a version -- or actually, this is a list of translation mistakes that I noticed. So when I checked the English translation, this is what I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will no longer need this exhibit. Given this observation and given the list of mistakes that you wrote, do you think that we can use your -- the English version, rather the translated version of your report for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: There's no problem. We can definitely use the English translation, but I would just like to mention, once again, that the French version should nevertheless be the authentic one, the one we should rely on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very well. Your report is divided in ten parts. The first portion of your report deals with your CV. So please take annex A of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 3D410 page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you find this exhibit, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What is it exactly?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It's my CV, curriculum vitae, my biography.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When was it made?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: In April of 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are there any changes that you would like to bring to your CV to update it?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I would just like to specify that I did not complete my doctoral thesis, and if everything goes well, I should obtain my Ph.D. by Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are there any other changes that you would like to mention?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: The one more small change is that I should mention that I should start teaching at McGill in January 2009 and the courses on Canada in foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to go back on some aspects of your CV, and I would like to ask you to confirm to us the following facts: You began working for the Canadian Armed Forces in 1978?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were within the forces for 34 years?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You retired in 2002?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you retired, your rank was lieutenant-colonel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What is your Ph.D. thesis, the thesis that you plan to finish by December?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Turbulence and Institutional Changes within the International Society, a Historic Perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you were within the Canadian Armed Forces, what was your classification as an officer?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I was a mechanized officer in the parachute division.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you are a St. Jean Royal Military College -- you obtained a diploma or degree, rather, from St. Jean Royal Military College?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how long did you study there?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: From 1973 to 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you obtain a diploma from this institution?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. First university cycle business administration, so a bachelors degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I see that from 1973 to 1975, you were a Mechanized Infantry Platoon commander within the 22nd Royal Regiment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And from 1975 to 1976, you served as an intelligence officer with the 1st Airborne Commando, Canadian Airborne Regiment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. And during this period, I also acted as the informations officer of the 1st Airborne Commando.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I also see that you were informations officer within the 1st Commando. Did you follow a specific training before you became an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. I followed an advanced intelligence course which lasted approximately three months. This course was dispensed to officers and majors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And between 1979 and 1982, you were a deputy commander and commander of Mechanized Infantry Company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Between 1982 and 1986, you served in the 1st Battalion Royal 22nd Regiment in Lahr in Germany, and you held the position of a captain?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During that period, did you also have other functions?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, I was a commander of the Canadian Forces Support unit for NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what does a commander of support company or support company commander does?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It offers support to an infantry platoon and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let him finish the answer please. Then we hear what you have to say, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't understand French, but we are not getting a full translation, and I note that the CV says "personnel officer" for this unit, and a command -- and the description we are getting of this job doesn't sound like a commander, but I just want to know if we have the translation right. Is he a personnel officer or a commander of this unit? But we are not getting a full translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. I think Mr. Bourgon will handle this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The CV of Mr. Landry says "personnel officer," indeed. That is why I put the question to him so he could explain what that is. The real position that he mentioned in French was "adjutant." Adjutant is a very specific position within any battalion, and it's like an executive assistant to the commander. That's, I think, what is the witness explained, but maybe the translation was not properly made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's first have a confirmation of what you've just stated by witness who, after all, is the one giving testimony. Colonel Landry, you followed what Mr. Bourgon has just said. Do you confirm that? Mr. Bourgon was also in the Canadian Army, so you should be speaking the same language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Does that satisfy you, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just so it's clear. He wasn't a commander, if that's the thrust of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understand it to be now. Yes. Okay. Go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Colonel, in 1987, I see that you were chosen to follow a 12 month long course at the Canadian Forces Command and Staff College in Toronto. My question is as follows: Who is this course destined to and what is the goal of this course?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: This course is for commanders that are just about to be promoted to the rank of lieutenant-colonel [as interpreted]. This course enables majors to learn the job, how to become a commander, and this course enables these same officers to evolve as a senior staff officer within headquarters of brigades, offering superior training and within the inter-army headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I would just like to bring a correction. On page 10 line 12, it is written in English that it is a course for commanders that are just about to be promoted to the rank of lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What did you say exactly.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is a course for majors, for majors. I should mention that the term "major" does not exist in French. So, in French, it's "commandant," "commander." Maybe that's why there was a mistake in the translation, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. From 1987 and 1989, you were the chief instructor at the Canadian Army Land Forces School; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In your CV, we see that you took part in an operational deployment while there were some internal troubles in Oka in 1989. Could you please tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Follow a crisis in a Mohawk reserve in the greater area of Montreal, they had erected barriers on national roads. They also took possession of a bridge, a major bridge, in Montreal, and following police actions which turned out to be fruitless, the provincial government asked the army to intervene in order to enable the -- to end the crisis basically. My implication at that time, I was deputy major of the battalion, and I was in charge of the city of Oka. So, basically, my deployment was trying to stabilize the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were promoted to a lieutenant-colonel in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Un moment, s'il vous plait. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think he meant deputy commander, but -- and it's important, so if that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you know, Mr. Bourgon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Colonel, the transcript says on page 11, line 12 that you were at the time a deputy major. What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I was the deputy commander -- "deputy commander" in English, and "commandant" in French - of the 1st Battalion of the 22nd Royal Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In 1993, you were a superior officer in the headquarters of the land forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in 1993, you were a member of the ECMM mission of the European Community deployed to Bosnia and Herzegovina, where you were deputy chief of mission for the regional centre of Zenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How long did this mission last?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During that mission, did you have the opportunity to see how the military forces operated -- the opposing military forces operated?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I was in a position to see the forces of the BiH army and the forces of the HVO and HV armies oppose in very difficult moments and very violent moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to see the Serb army of Bosnia operate?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, indirectly, following the actions taken by the BiH army to counter the advances or prepare offences against the Serb army. And in my frequent contacts with the staff officers of UNPROFOR, I could get acquainted with the nature of the operations led by the Serbs at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned "UNPROFOR." What exactly is it?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It was the supposedly peacekeeping mission for the whole of Bosnia Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your mission in Bosnia Herzegovina, did it allow you to draw any conclusions regarding the operations of the opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: One of my first findings was to realise the fact that the three armies in presence used the same doctrine, which was the former doctrine of the Yugoslav Army amongst others. I also was in a position to get acquainted with the geography of Bosnia Herzegovina because I took -- well, I travelled many times between Mostar and Tuzla, and I also got to know the way the 3rd Bosnia Corps operated. And even on some occasions, I supervised or came into contact with the authorities of the 2nd Camp because I was familiar with their positions in the greater region of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you have the feeling, Colonel, that you have a good enough knowledge of the Serb army in Bosnia to be able to answer or give truthful answers to the questions you were asked in your report?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I think that given my experience in Bosnia that I was in a position, given the test I was entrusted with, to give a good analysis of the military doctrine of the armies that were present; and that given my military education, given my subsequent experiences, and as a result of my different interventions here and of my education in general, I do think that I am in a position to be able to do what I was asked to do, i.e., to analyse the leadership aspects and military professionalism aspects of the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I pause, it's to allow the interpreters to be able to follow the rhythm of the questions and answers. So, Colonel, without naming anybody or giving us a period of time during which were covered by your report, what is the main topic in your report?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: You asked me to analyse a testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, let me specify. What subject matter is your report all about?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It's about how operations were led in and around Zvornik in the period of time that covers 13th to 15th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll have the opportunity to come back to this. In 1997, you were transferred to the Peace Academy in New York. Now, what is this exactly?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: The International Peace Academy is, before anything else, a think-tank that is set up to serve the UN and that analyses peace operations and peacekeeping operations initiated by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On page 14, it appears before you on line 6, it is said the period covered by your report is July 13th to 15th. Did you mention those dates?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I saw that you got many awards in your resume; namely, one that is the award for Military Order?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It is one of the distinctions given by the Canadian army by the Governor General that is given to some military officers for their professionalism all over their career.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To come back to my former question: Did you analyse the day of July 12th, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I analysed the 12th, the 13th, the 14th, and the 15th of July in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On page 3 of your resume, I see that you followed several courses during your career, which was the purpose of these courses you followed.

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: It was greatly or mostly to allow me as an officer to get a better understanding of the armed forces in general and the profession in the armed forces, and to be able to operate in any functions that can be found inside mechanized infantry battalions or inside an airborne unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In 2002, I see that you chose to follow in academic course. What about your masters degree which you got in 1997, can you tell us more about that?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Following my stay in Bosnia in 1993, the Canadian Air Forces offered me to follow a masters programme, which I initiated and completed. I got a masters in political sciences, and my topic was "The Origins of the Conflict in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, today, Colonel, you are a consultant in security issues and military analyst for different media and other organizations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the basis of your experience, I can see that you were called to testify on two occasions in this Tribunal. In which cases did you testify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection for leading on -- because it's unclear whether he has been called as an expert or what. So if he could be clear on, you know, why he was called in those cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon, I think you can handle this. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is the question I'm going to ask to the witness. I don't see the point of the objection, but I thank my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In which cases did you testify, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: According to your CV, you testified in two occasions before this Court in two cases. Which are they?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: The first one is in the Blasic case, and second one is Mr. Kordic as a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who called you to testify in these cases?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: The Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have the occasion to work on any other case in this Court?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity to work with you awhile ago in the case of General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What were you asked to do on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: I was mainly asked to advise you on the testimony of the expert witness called by the Prosecutor, i.e., General Reinhold, former commander of the Allied Forces in Europe, and to be able to give you some advice on the military aspects of the other witnesses who testified in that case for the period that I was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the completion of those tasks, did you have the opportunity of studying any further the doctrine of the former Yugoslavia army?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I did. In order to be able to give you better advice, I had at the time to take an in-depth look at the doctrinal aspects of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As a lecturer at the university, I see that you taught military ethics and leadership. When was this and what exactly is this about?

utterances.speaker: REMI LANDRY
utterances.text: These are courses of professional development for officers, and at the time, I was asked to teach at the Kingston Royal Military College, the French section of the Montreal region. This was done in 2001 and 2004, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we can now move into private session for the continuation of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are going to do that immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, we are resuming this after the break. We will revert immediately to private session as explained for the reasons explained earlier on. So let's go into private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yesterday, before we adjourned we heard, Mr. Josse saying that he did not have any further reservations about the Miletic motion of the 18th of September, seeking authorisation to add some documents to the list of exhibits to the 65 ter list of exhibits. I will put the question again. Prosecution, we know already, haven't got any objection. Anyone else has any objection? No objections. So the motion is being granted orally now. Then, Mr. McCloskey, we are not asking you to give your position now or imposing any dates for the time being, but there are three new Borovcanin motions which we would like you to give your attention to as early as possible, keeping in mind that the Borovcanin Defence supposedly should start on the 6th of October. Right. Take your time, but as soon as you are in a position to give us your response, let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have been talking about counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
